decision.explanation: For y=x^r, the characteristic equation is 2r(r-1)-r+1=(2r-1)(r-1)=0. Thus y=C_1x+C_2√x. The initial conditions give C_1+C_2=0 and C_1+C_2/2=1, so C_1=2 and C_2=-2. Therefore y(x)=2x-2√x, option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\lambda =1.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{1/2}+{c}_{2}{x}^{1}={c}_{1}\sqrt{x}+{c}_{2}x.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2\sqrt{x}}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+{c}_{2} \\ 2 & ={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ 2 & ={c}_{1}-2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =-2\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=2x-2\sqrt{x}.
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem 2x2y″−xy′+y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=1,x>0.

a
y(x)=x45−15x
b
y(x)=x34−14x
c

d
y(x)=2x−2x
e
 y(x)=xln⁡x

EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

2x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2−x⋅λxλ−1+xλ=02λ(λ−1)xλ−λxλ+xλ=0xλ[2λ(λ−1)−λ+1]=0.

The auxiliary equation is 2λ(λ−1)−λ+1=02λ2−3λ+1=0(2λ−1)(λ−1)=0.

Hence, the roots are λ=12 and λ=1. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=c1x1/2+c2x1=c1x+c2x.

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=0 into the general solution gives 0=c1+c2⇒c2=−c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=1. First, we differentiate y to find y′: y′=c12x+c2

Substituting y′(1)=1 into the above gives 1=c12+c22=c1+2c22=c1−2c1c1=−2⇒c2=2.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=2x−2x.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +1 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\lambda =1.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{1/2}+{c}_{2}{x}^{1}={c}_{1}\sqrt{x}+{c}_{2}x.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2\sqrt{x}}+{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+{c}_{2} \\ 2 & ={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2} \\ 2 & ={c}_{1}-2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =-2\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=2x-2\sqrt{x}.
$$

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}-4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }-4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -4] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda +2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2{c}_{1}x-2\frac{{c}_{2}}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}

Question 3
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem 4x2y″+8xy′−3y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=2,x>0.

a
y(x)=x3/2+x−1/2
b
y(x)=x1/2−x−3/2
c
y(x)=−2x−3/2
d
y(x)=−2x1/2+x−3/2
e
y(x)=2x1/2+x−1/2
Submit

decision.explanation: With y=x^r, the characteristic equation is 4r(r-1)+8r-3=(2r-1)(2r+3)=0. Thus y=C_1x^{1/2}+C_2x^{-3/2}. The initial conditions give C_1+C_2=0 and C_1/2-3C_2/2=2, yielding C_1=1 and C_2=-1. Therefore option b satisfies the initial value problem.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
4{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+8x{y}^{′}-3y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+8x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}-3{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 4\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+8\lambda {x}^{\lambda }-3{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[4\lambda (\lambda -1)+8\lambda -3] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda (\lambda -1)+8\lambda -3 & =0 \\ 4{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(2\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\lambda =-\frac{3}{2}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{1/2}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{c}_{1}{x}^{-1/2}}{2}-\frac{3{c}_{2}{x}^{-5/2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}-\frac{3{c}_{2}}{2} \\ 2 & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}-\frac{3(-{c}_{1})}{2} \\ 2 & =2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =1\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)={x}^{1/2}-{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Question 3
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem 4x2y″+8xy′−3y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=2,x>0.

a
y(x)=x3/2+x−1/2
b
y(x)=x1/2−x−3/2
c
y(x)=−2x−3/2
d
y(x)=−2x1/2+x−3/2
e
y(x)=2x1/2+x−1/2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

4x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+8x⋅λxλ−1−3xλ=04λ(λ−1)xλ+8λxλ−3xλ=0xλ[4λ(λ−1)+8λ−3]=0.

The auxiliary equation is 4λ(λ−1)+8λ−3=04λ2+4λ−3=0(2λ−1)(2λ+3)=0.

Hence, the roots are λ=12 and λ=−32. Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=c1x1/2+c2x−3/2.

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=0 into the general solution gives 0=c1+c2⇒c2=−c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=2. First, we differentiate y to find y′: y′=c1x−1/22−3c2x−5/22

Substituting y′(1)=1 into the above gives 2=c12−3c222=c12−3(−c1)22=2c1c1=1⇒c2=−1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=x1/2−x−3/2.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
4{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+8x{y}^{′}-3y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+8x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}-3{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 4\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+8\lambda {x}^{\lambda }-3{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[4\lambda (\lambda -1)+8\lambda -3] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}4\lambda (\lambda -1)+8\lambda -3 & =0 \\ 4{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (2\lambda -1)(2\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ and $\lambda =-\frac{3}{2}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{1/2}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=2.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{c}_{1}{x}^{-1/2}}{2}-\frac{3{c}_{2}{x}^{-5/2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}-\frac{3{c}_{2}}{2} \\ 2 & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}-\frac{3(-{c}_{1})}{2} \\ 2 & =2{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & =1\,⇒\,{c}_{2}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)={x}^{1/2}-{x}^{-3/2}.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}-3y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}-3{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }-3{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -3] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -3 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(2\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-1$ and $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-1}+{c}_{2}{t}^{3/2}.
$$

Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}-3y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}-3{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }-3{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -3] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda -3 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -3 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(2\lambda -3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-1$ and $\lambda =\frac{3}{2}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}{t}^{-1}+{c}_{2}{t}^{3/2}.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Instance of the Cauchy-Euler Equation
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+6x{y}^{′}+6y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+6x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+6{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+6\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+6{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+6\lambda +6] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+6\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+5\lambda +6 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)(\lambda +3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2$ and $\lambda =-3.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}{x}^{-2}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-3}.
$$
